title: Duty of candour: disclosing a bile duct injury

header.contentArea: Communication skills in giving and receiving information and history taking
guidelineVersions: GMC/NMC Openness and honesty when things go wrong (in effect 29 Jun 2015; updated 13 Dec 2024)
Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, reg 20

related.id: MB-160 Consent: emergency laparotomy and possible stoma
related.why: Discussing risks before treatment, which the candour guidance builds on

brief.role: Core surgical trainee on the general surgical team
brief.scenario: Mrs Doreen Kettley, 68, had an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy four days ago. A bile duct injury was recognised and repaired during the operation, but afterwards she was told only that it "went well". She now has a bile leak on MRCP and needs an ERCP. Your consultant, Miss Hale, would normally lead this conversation but is operating; she has asked you to begin it now and will meet the family later today.
brief.task: Speak to Mrs Kettley and her daughter. Explain what has happened, apologise, and explain what happens next.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Honest disclosure with an early, personal apology, then a plan.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Waiting for an investigation, minimising, or blaming the surgeon.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Sit down, check who she wants present, and find out what she knows.

grid.label: Opening and setting
grid.fail: Starts talking in the corridor or standing up; does not ask who the daughter is or whether Mrs Kettley wants her present.
grid.pass: Introduces self and role, sits down, asks who is present and if she wants her daughter to stay, checks what she knows.
grid.high: Also explains the consultant is in theatre, asked them to start now rather than wait, and will see them later today.

grid.label: Telling her what happened, plainly
grid.fail: Uses jargon or minimising words ("small leak", "a bit of a hiccup"); does not say the injury happened during the operation.
grid.pass: Warning shot, then plain words: the bile duct was injured during the operation, repaired at the time, and bile is now leaking.
grid.high: Separates what is known from what is not yet established, and says so honestly rather than guessing why it happened.

grid.label: Apology
grid.fail: No apology, "sorry you feel that way", or blames the operating surgeon.
grid.pass: Early, personal apology ("I am sorry") for what happened, not for her feelings.
grid.high: Also apologises that she was told the operation went well; does not blame colleagues; explains why it matters that she knows.

grid.label: Next steps and effects
grid.fail: "The team will sort it out"; no plan, or promises the outcome.
grid.pass: Explains ERCP: a camera through the mouth places a stent so bile drains into the bowel and the leak can heal.
grid.high: Adds drainage and antibiotics if needed, the stent removed later by another ERCP, and follow-up for later narrowing of the duct.

grid.label: Responding to distress and anger
grid.fail: Talks over the daughter's anger, becomes defensive, or ignores tears.
grid.pass: Pauses, names the emotion, lets them speak, and acknowledges the anger is understandable.
grid.high: Answers "are you covering up?" directly: everything known is being shared, and the consultant will explain the operation.

grid.label: Organisational candour and support
grid.fail: Says nothing about reporting, or implies a written account is only if she asks.
grid.pass: Incident is being reported; the trust will follow this conversation with a written account and apology (Regulation 20).
grid.high: Explains any further enquiries and that results will be shared; offers PALS and independent support such as AvMA.

grid.label: Liability, record and close
grid.fail: Refuses to apologise "for legal reasons", or leaves without checking understanding or recording the conversation.
grid.pass: Checks understanding, gives a named contact, records the conversation and apology in the notes, informs the consultant.
grid.high: States an apology is not an admission of liability and does not affect their right to raise concerns or seek advice.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Mrs Kettley: "They said the operation went well. When can I go home?"

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Hi, I'm from the surgical team. There's been a bit of a hiccup. The scan shows a small bile leak, which happens sometimes after this operation.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Daughter: "A leak? Did someone make a mistake? Why weren't we told?"

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I wasn't in theatre, so I can't comment on what the surgeon did. You'd have to ask them.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The team will sort it out, she'll be fine. We can't really say sorry because of the legal side, but if you want something in writing you can ask.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Someone will come and explain later. I'll ask the nurse to bring some painkillers.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical trainees. May I sit down? Who is with you today? Are you happy for your daughter to stay while we talk? What have you been told since the operation?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Mrs Kettley: "That it went well. But I feel sick and sore."

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'm afraid I have some difficult news. During your operation, the tube that carries bile from the liver, the bile duct, was injured. The surgeon repaired it at the time, but a scan shows bile is leaking. That is why you feel unwell. I am very sorry this has happened.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Daughter: "Why were we told it went well?"

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: You have every right to be upset. Please tell me what's worrying you most.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The plan is a procedure called an ERCP: a camera passed through the mouth places a small tube, a stent, so bile drains into the bowel and the leak can heal.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This is being reported as an incident. After today the hospital will write to you with an account of what happened and an apology.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Could you tell me what you've understood? The ward sister is your contact. I'll write this conversation and my apology in your notes and update the consultant.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, a surgical trainee on Miss Hale's team. May I sit? Who's with you, and would you like your daughter to stay? Miss Hale is operating this morning; she asked me to talk to you now rather than make you wait, and she will come to see you both this afternoon. First, what have you been told?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Mrs Kettley: "That it went well. But I feel awful."

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'm afraid I have some difficult news. During your operation the bile duct, the tube that carries bile from the liver, was injured. The surgeon saw it and repaired it, but a scan shows bile is leaking, which is why you feel unwell. I am very sorry. I'm also sorry you were told it went well; you should have been told straight away. We know about the injury and the leak. Why it happened is not yet established, and I won't guess.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I can see how angry you are, and I understand why. No. I've told you everything we know, and Miss Hale will explain the operation herself.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Next is an ERCP to place a stent so the leak can heal; if fluid has collected we may drain it, with antibiotics. The stent is taken out later with another ERCP, and we'll follow you up because the duct can narrow over time.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This is being reported, and the hospital will look into what happened, share the results with you, and write to you with an apology. PALS or an independent charity such as AvMA can support you.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Saying sorry isn't admitting legal liability, and it doesn't stop you raising concerns. What have you understood? The ward sister is your contact. I'll record this conversation and my apology.

failures.move: Calling it "a small leak that happens sometimes".
failures.consequence: She later learns the duct was injured and feels misled a second time; trust is harder to rebuild.

failures.move: Saying "I wasn't there, ask the surgeon" instead of apologising.
failures.consequence: She is entitled to an apology from the team regardless of who was responsible; deflecting sounds like concealment.

failures.move: Telling her she can have something in writing "if she wants".
failures.consequence: For a notifiable safety incident the trust must follow the in-person notification with a written one that includes an apology.
An apology is not of itself an admission of negligence; withholding it damages trust.

recovery.line: Let me put that more simply: the tube that carries bile from your liver was damaged during the operation.

recovery.when: "Why were we told it went well?"
recovery.line: You should have been told straight away, and I'm sorry you weren't. I want to make sure you know everything now.
That isn't established yet. It is being looked into, and you will be told what is found.

knowledge.fact: The lead or accountable clinician usually speaks to the patient; if that is not you, make sure someone in the team has taken this on and support them.
Speak as soon as possible; do not wait for an investigation, but say what is and is not yet established.
An apology covers what happened, what can be done about the harm, and what will be done to prevent it happening again.
For a notifiable safety incident the trust must tell the patient in person as soon as reasonably practicable, apologise, keep a record, and follow up in writing.
In England and Wales an apology is not of itself an admission of negligence; NHS Resolution will never refuse cover because an apology was given.

recall.think: Honesty now protects her trust and her care.
recall.say: "During your operation the bile duct was injured. I am very sorry."

numbers.meaning: parts of an apology: what happened, dealing with harm, prevention
in-person notification must be followed in writing, with an apology
Compensation Act: apology is not an admission of negligence

recall.trap: Waiting for the investigation, or saying "ask the surgeon".
recall.finish: Consultant meets the family today; written notification follows.

sources.name: GMC and NMC: Openness and honesty when things go wrong: the professional duty of candour
sources.version: In effect 29 June 2015; last updated 13 December 2024
sources.supports: Tell, apologise, offer remedy, explain short- and long-term effects (introductory statement); make sure someone in the team takes responsibility (para 6); the lead or accountable clinician is usually the most appropriate person to speak to the patient (para 10); speak as soon as possible, with support available; no need to wait for an investigation, but be clear what is and is not established (para 11); share what is known and what is uncertain, answer honestly (para 12); an apology covers what happened, what can be done about the harm, and prevention (para 14); apology is not an admission of legal liability (para 15); no personal blame required for others' errors (para 16); personalised apology, named contact, independent advocacy and support, record the apology, written apology depending on wishes and workplace policy (para 17); report incidents through local and national systems (paras 24-26)

sources.name: Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 (SI 2014/2936), regulation 20: Duty of candour
sources.version: Made 6 November 2014; revised text valid from 7 September 2026 (legislation.gov.uk)
sources.supports: Organisational duty (England): as soon as reasonably practicable after a notifiable safety incident, notify the relevant person in person, give a true account of the known facts, advise what further enquiries are appropriate, include an apology, and keep a written record (reg 20(2)-(3)); this must be followed by written notification with the same account, details and results of enquiries, and an apology (reg 20(4)); moderate harm includes an unplanned return to surgery, a prolonged episode of care or extra time in hospital (reg 20(7))

sources.name: Compensation Act 2006 (c. 29), section 2
sources.supports: An apology, an offer of treatment or other redress, shall not of itself amount to an admission of negligence or breach of statutory duty

sources.name: NHS Resolution: Saying sorry (leaflet)
sources.supports: Saying sorry is the right thing to do; NHS Resolution will never refuse cover on a claim because an apology has been given

sources.name: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery (O'Connell, McCaskie, Sayers, eds)
sources.supports: Bile duct injury as a recognised complication of laparoscopic cholecystectomy; post-operative bile leak managed by ERCP with biliary stenting and drainage of any collection; later stricture as a long-term risk needing follow-up

partner.opening: Mrs Kettley is sitting in bed with her daughter, Joanne. Please begin when you're ready.
partner.actorBrief: Two roles. DOREEN KETTLEY, 68, retired school secretary, lives alone, independent. You had your gallbladder removed four days ago; you were told it "went well". Since then you have felt sick, sore and feverish, and nobody has told you why. You are tired and trusting, and become tearful when you hear the news. Hidden worry: you look after your grandson after school and fear you won't cope. If asked what she knows: "They said it went well. But I feel awful." JOANNE, 42, her daughter, a practice manager. Protective and quick to anger. After the disclosure: "Why were we told it went well?" If the candidate is vague or defensive, ask "Are you covering this up?" If the candidate apologises sincerely and is straightforward, calm down and ask practical questions. Ask "Is this going to affect her long term?" if the candidate does not cover it. Both accept the plan if it is explained clearly. If asked to explain back, give a fair summary.

reveals.trigger: Asks who is present and whether Doreen wants her daughter there
reveals.finding: "Yes, I want Joanne here. She's better with doctors than me."

reveals.trigger: Asks what she has been told
reveals.finding: "That it went well. But I've been sick and sore, and hot at night."
Doreen: "I look after my grandson after school. How will I manage?"
Joanne: "So we'll get this in writing? Good."
"The tube was damaged, they fixed it but it's leaking, and a camera test will put a little tube in to let it heal."

push.question: Who should normally lead this conversation, and why are you starting it?
push.expect: The consultant as lead or accountable clinician; she is in theatre and asked the trainee to begin so the family is not kept waiting; she will meet them later today.

push.question: What does the trust have to do after today's conversation?
push.expect: Record the notification and follow it with written notification: the account of the facts, further enquiries and their results, and an apology.

curveballs.safeAnswer: That is not yet established; it is being looked into, the results will be shared, and the consultant will explain the operation in person.

curveballs.prompt: Joanne: "We're going to see a solicitor."
curveballs.safeAnswer: That is your right. Saying sorry is not admitting liability, and it doesn't change your options; PALS or AvMA can advise.

curveballs.prompt: Doreen: "Is this going to affect me long term?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: We expect the leak to heal once bile drains through the stent; the duct can narrow later, so she will be followed up and told what to watch for.
